transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Hurst.
President Trump says he's replacing Susie Wiles
as White House Chief of Staff with Stephen Miller,
who's currently the Deputy Chief of Staff.
Stephen's been with me from the beginning.
He gets it very good politically, and he's a very good man.
He'll do a great job, great manager.
As NPR's Daniel Kurtzleben reports,
it signals a White House that isn't backing down
after blistering Republican losses
in this year's midterm elections.
President Trump announced the personnel change
on social media, saying Miller will take over
the position on Monday, November 9th.
Wiles worked with the Trump 2020 campaign in Florida
and has served as Chief of Staff in this White House
from day one of this administration.
She's the first woman to hold the position.
In his social media post, Trump says
she will be moving to the Trump political operation.
Miller has been a fixture in Trump's circle since 2016
and is considered one of the President's most trusted
and aggressive advisors.
He is known in particular for being an architect
of the President's anti-immigration policies.
Danielle Kurtzleben, NPR News, the White House.
The city of Houston will see a reduction
in immigration enforcement after Democratic victories
in Texas elections this week.
Houston Public Media's Sarah Grunow has more.
Houston Mayor John Whitmire is directing
Houston Police Department officers to reduce
their contact with immigration and customs enforcement.
That means officers in Houston will no longer
be allowed to detain people solely based
on civil immigration warrants.
I do this to begin a healing process,
reduce fear and anxiety across our community.
I also do this knowing that elections matter.
It's a stark difference from previous policy
on police interacting with ICE,
which has drawn scrutiny and protests over the past year.
Previously, state officials blocked Houston
from limiting its cooperation with ICE,
threatening to withhold millions in public safety funding.
I'm Sarah Grunow in Houston.
Employers in the U.S. added 165,000 jobs in October,
far more than analysts had been expecting,
and Pierre Scott Horsley has more.
A new report from the Labor Department shows
significantly stronger job growth
than forecasters had expected for October.
Job gains for August and September were also revised up.
Industries adding jobs last month include health care,
transportation and professional services.
Restaurants cut workers in October,
as did construction companies.
The unemployment rate inched down to 4.1 percent,
even as hundreds of thousands of new people
joined the workforce.
The stronger job market also shows up in bigger wage gains.
Wages in October were up 3.1 percent from a year ago.
That's a bigger annual increase than the previous month,
but still probably not enough to keep pace with rising prices.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
Wall Street mixed by the closing bell.
You're listening to NPR News.
Developing and distributing COVID-19 vaccines
cost billions of dollars.
But as NPR's Jonathan Lambert reports,
new research suggests it generated trillions of dollars
in health and economic benefits around the world.
Creating a vaccine against an entirely new virus within a year
was an incredible scientific feat.
And expensive.
Through 2021, it cost nearly 80 billion dollars.
New research in the journal PLOS Medicine
tried to figure out whether, from an economic perspective,
the cost was worth it.
Researchers gathered data on the impact of vaccines
in terms of infections and deaths averted.
They then translated that into economic benefits
in terms of productivity gained from workers
not getting sick or dying.
They estimate that for every dollar spent on vaccines,
there were about 60 to 800 dollars in return benefit.
Those benefits weren't equally distributed, however.
Wealthier countries, who got earlier access to the vaccines,
tended to have higher economic benefits
than lower-income countries.
Jonathan Lambert, NPR News.
Pope Leo is in Uruguay starting a three-nation tour of South America.
It comes less than a month after lung cancer surgery
that had thrown the 12-day trip into question.
And it marks the first papal visit to the country in nearly 40 years.
Leo was greeted by throngs of people lining his motorcade route
under cloudy, windy skies,
cheering as his open-sided Pope mobile passed by.
Uruguay is known for its secularism,
having separated church and state.
More than 100 years ago,
Leo hopes to reconnect the country with its Catholic roots.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.

topics.text: President Trump names Stephen Miller White House Chief of Staff, replacing Susie Wiles
Houston Mayor John Whitmire limits police cooperation with ICE on civil immigration warrants
US employers add 165,000 jobs in October, well above analyst expectations
New research finds COVID-19 vaccines generated trillions in global health and economic benefits
Pope Leo arrives in Uruguay to begin three-nation South America tour
